lead: Setting out turns a design into marks on the ground. It reverses a topographical survey: control points already have known coordinates, and the crew places a new point at its design coordinates by angle and distance. A foundation, column, road centreline or drain must sit where the drawing says, not where the ground suggests. Total station stakeout and GNSS stakeout are the two common methods. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic; most fold it into engineering surveying.
prereq: You need 5.1 Total station and the control ideas of Unit 4, Horizontal and vertical control.

blocks.text: Setting out, also called layout surveying, places a designed point on the ground from known control. A control point is a fixed station with known coordinates and level. The design gives the target as coordinates (E, N), where E is easting and N is northing, or as an offset from a reference line. A reference line is a straight baseline between two known points, such as a building grid line or road centreline.

Horizontal control fixes easting and northing; vertical control fixes reduced level. The crew sets the instrument on a control station and orients it to a backsight, a second known station. The instrument now has a known zero direction. The crew turns the computed angle and measures the computed distance.

The coordinate method stores control and target coordinates in the total station. The angle-distance method computes azimuth and distance first. GNSS stakeout works in open sky; a total station is better near walls or under trees. See 5.1 and 5.2.

sections.h3: From coordinates to a peg, then a check

blocks.text: ΔE = E_target − E_station; ΔN = N_target − N_station; α = atan2(ΔE, ΔN); D = √(ΔE² + ΔN²); β = α_target − α_backsight
blocks.where: ΔE and ΔN are easting and northing differences in metres; α is azimuth clockwise from north, with atan2 taking easting first; D is horizontal distance; β is the setting-out angle from the backsight, reduced to 0° to 360°.

blocks.text: Field steps: set on the control station, sight the backsight, set that direction as β = 0°, turn β clockwise, measure D, and drive the peg. Check from another control station; one setup cannot reveal an orientation blunder.

Construction surveys repeat this at each stage: site clearing, foundation corners, columns, road centreline, drainage gradients, and deformation monitoring. Tolerances come from the project specification. An as-built check re-measures the finished work independently and records actual coordinates. GNSS stakeout is fast in open areas; total station stakeout is stronger in urban or covered sites.

examples.question: Control station A is (E 1000.000 m, N 1000.000 m) with backsight azimuth 0°00′00″. A building corner C is to be set at (E 1025.000 m, N 1040.000 m). Find the setting-out angle from the backsight and the horizontal distance AC.
steps: Both positive: C is north-east of A, so α lies between 0° and 90°.
examples.answer: Turn 32.00538° clockwise from the backsight and measure 47.170 m horizontally from A to peg C.
examples.check:
import math
E_A, N_A = 1000.000, 1000.000
E_C, N_C = 1025.000, 1040.000
dE = E_C - E_A
dN = N_C - N_A
D = math.hypot(dE, dN)
az = math.degrees(math.atan2(dE, dN)) % 360
print(f"{dE:.3f}")
print(f"{dN:.3f}")
print(f"{D:.3f}")
print(f"{az:.5f}")

traps: Swapping easting and northing in atan2. Use atan2(ΔE, ΔN), not atan2(ΔN, ΔE).
Using a magnetic bearing as a grid azimuth. Magnetic bearings carry declination and local attraction; setting out needs project or grid azimuth.
Forgetting the backsight. β = target azimuth − backsight azimuth, reduced to 0–360°.
Laying out slope distance as horizontal distance. Reduce EDM slope distance before marking.
Checking only from the setup that set the peg. Re-measure from another control point to catch orientation and coordinate blunders.

quiz.a: Placing a designed point on the ground from known control coordinates by angle and distance.

quiz.q: Why is a backsight needed before turning a setting-out angle?
quiz.a: It gives a known zero direction; without it, angles are relative to an arbitrary instrument zero.

quiz.q: A is (500.000 m, 500.000 m) and B is (530.000 m, 540.000 m). Find azimuth and horizontal distance AB.
A peg is set from A using B as backsight, but B's northing is wrong by 1 m. What happens and how is it detected?
quiz.a: All bearings from A rotate, so the peg shifts mostly perpendicular to the sight. Checking from a second control point or a third known point detects it.

quiz.q: Backsight azimuth is 120°00′00″ and target azimuth is 75°00′00″. What angle is turned?
quiz.a: β = 75° − 120° = −45°; add 360° to get 315° clockwise, or turn 45° anticlockwise.

quiz.q: GNSS or total station for stakeout beside a tall building?
quiz.a: Total station; GNSS needs open sky and suffers multipath near walls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Robotic total stations and GNSS-RTK networks now send stakeout commands from a tablet, and machine-control graders use the same coordinates to cut a road formation. BIM and digital twins feed design coordinates straight to the field and store as-built positions back into the model. Deformation monitoring repeats setting-out checks on dams, slopes and metro tunnels. Search for robotic total station stakeout, GNSS RTK, BIM-to-field layout, and automated deformation monitoring.
